claim: Progress in science requires standardized assays whose results can be readily shared, compared, and reproduced across laboratories.
source: Progress in science requires standardized assays whose results can be readily shared, compared, and reproduced across laboratories.
evidence: This is a general statement about scientific methodology presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: Reproducibility has been a concern in neuroscience, particularly for measurements of mouse behavior.
source: Reproducibility, however, has been a concern in neuroscience, particularly for measurements of mouse behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: A standardized task to probe decision-making in mice produces reproducible results across multiple laboratories.
source: Here, we show that a standardized task to probe decision-making in mice produces reproducible results across multiple laboratories.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data collected across seven laboratories.

claim: The study trained 140 mice across seven laboratories in three countries.
source: We trained 140 mice across seven laboratories in three countries, and we collected 5 million mouse choices into a publicly available database.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental scope, supported by the data collection described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study collected 5 million mouse choices into a publicly available database.
source: We trained 140 mice across seven laboratories in three countries, and we collected 5 million mouse choices into a publicly available database.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size, supported by the data collection and sharing infrastructure described in the manuscript.

claim: Learning speed was variable across mice and laboratories.
source: Learning speed was variable across mice and laboratories, but once training was complete there were no significant differences in behavior across laboratories.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating variability in training times.

claim: Once training was complete there were no significant differences in behavior across laboratories.
source: Learning speed was variable across mice and laboratories, but once training was complete there were no significant differences in behavior across laboratories.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses and data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on visual stimuli to guide their choices.
source: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on visual stimuli, on past successes and failures, and on estimates of stimulus prior probability to guide their choices.
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on past successes and failures to guide their choices.
source: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on visual stimuli, on past successes and failures, and on estimates of stimulus prior probability to guide their choices.
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on estimates of stimulus prior probability to guide their choices.
source: Mice in different laboratories adopted similar reliance on visual stimuli, on past successes and failures, and on estimates of stimulus prior probability to guide their choices.
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5 and the block structure analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Standardized assays are common in fields such as astronomy, physics, genetics, and medicine.
source: Such assays are common in fields such as astronomy (Fish et al., 2016; Abdalla et al., 2018), physics (CERN Education, Communications and Outreach Group, 2018), genetics (Dickinson et al., 2016), and medicine (Bycroft et al., 2018), and perhaps rarer in fields such as sociology (Camerer et al., 2018) and psychology (Forscher et al., 2020; Frank et al., 2017; Makel et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to work in these fields.

claim: Standardized assays are rarer in fields such as sociology and psychology.
source: Such assays are common in fields such as astronomy (Fish et al., 2016; Abdalla et al., 2018), physics (CERN Education, Communications and Outreach Group, 2018), genetics (Dickinson et al., 2016), and medicine (Bycroft et al., 2018), and perhaps rarer in fields such as sociology (Camerer et al., 2018) and psychology (Forscher et al., 2020; Frank et al., 2017; Makel et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to work discussing reproducibility in these fields.

claim: Standardized assays are rare in neuroscience.
source: They are also rare in neuroscience, a field that faces a reproducibility crisis (Baker, 2016; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020; Button et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on the reproducibility crisis in neuroscience.

claim: Neuroscience faces a reproducibility crisis.
source: They are also rare in neuroscience, a field that faces a reproducibility crisis (Baker, 2016; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020; Button et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature documenting reproducibility issues in neuroscience.

claim: Reproducibility has been a particular concern for measurements of mouse behavior.
source: Reproducibility has been a particular concern for measurements of mouse behavior (Kafkafi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to work on mouse behavior reproducibility.

claim: Methods can be generally reproduced across laboratories, but results can be surprisingly different.
source: Although the methods can be generally reproduced across laboratories, the results can be surprisingly different ('methods reproducibility' vs. 'results reproducibility', Goodman et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation distinguishing types of reproducibility.

claim: Even seemingly simple assays of responses to pain or stress can be swayed by extraneous factors.
source: Even seemingly simple assays of responses to pain or stress can be swayed by extraneous factors (Chesler et al., 2002; Crabbe et al., 1999) such as the sex of the experimenter (Sorge et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies showing effects of extraneous factors on mouse behavior.

claim: The sex of the experimenter can affect mouse behavioral assays.
source: Even seemingly simple assays of responses to pain or stress can be swayed by extraneous factors (Chesler et al., 2002; Crabbe et al., 1999) such as the sex of the experimenter (Sorge et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this effect.

claim: Behavioral assays can be difficult to reproduce across laboratories even when they share a similar apparatus.
source: Behavioral assays can be difficult to reproduce across laboratories even when they share a similar apparatus (Chesler et al., 2002; Crabbe et al., 1999; Sorge et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies documenting reproducibility challenges.

claim: Behavioral variability is as large in inbred mice as in outbred mice.
source: This difficulty is not simply due to genetic variation: behavioral variability is as large in inbred mice as in outbred mice (Tuttle et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a study comparing behavioral variability in inbred and outbred mice.

claim: Physiological studies of decision making are increasingly carried out in mice to access genetic, imaging, and physiological tools.
source: Physiological studies of decision making are increasingly carried out in mice to access the unrivaled arsenal of genetic, imaging, and physiological tools available for mouse brains (Carandini and Churchland, 2013; Glickfeld et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies using mice for decision-making research.

claim: The International Brain Laboratory aims to explore the neural basis of mouse behavior in multiple laboratories.
source: Our collaboration, International Brain Laboratory, 2017, aims to leverage these approaches by exploring the neural basis of the same mouse behavior in multiple laboratories.
evidence: This is a statement about the goals of the collaboration conducting this research.

claim: It is crucial for the International Brain Laboratory that behavioral assays be reproducible both in methods and in results.
source: It is thus crucial for this endeavor that the relevant behavioral assays be reproducible both in methods and in results.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for the collaboration's research goals.

claim: The task should be complex enough to expose neural computations that support decision-making but simple enough for mice to learn.
source: The task should be complex enough to expose the neural computations that support decision-making but simple enough for mice to learn, and easily extendable to study further aspects of perception and cognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the design criteria for the behavioral task.

claim: Head fixation provides ready access to the brain for neural recordings and manipulations.
source: Moreover, it can be invaluable to have ready access to the brain for neural recordings and manipulations, a consideration that favors tasks that involve head fixation.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of head-fixed tasks for neuroscience research.

claim: The study adopted a modified version of the classical 'two-alternative forced-choice' perceptual detection task.
source: To meet these criteria, we adopted a modified version of the classical 'two-alternative forced-choice' perceptual detection task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design used in the study.

claim: In the classical task, the subject indicates the position of a stimulus that can be in one of two positions with equal probability.
source: In the classical task, the subject indicates the position of a stimulus that can be in one of two positions with equal probability (e.g. Carandini and Churchland, 2013; Tanner and Swets, 1954).
evidence: This statement describes the classical task and is supported by citations.

claim: In the modified version, the probability of the stimulus being in one position changes over time.
source: In the modified version, the probability of the stimulus being in one position changes over time (Terman and Terman, 1972).
evidence: This statement describes the modification to the task and is supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in probability may affect sensory decisions by directing spatial attention.
source: This change in probability may affect sensory decisions by directing spatial attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Liston and Stone, 2008) and by biasing the decision process (Hanks et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on attention and decision-making.

claim: Changes in probability may affect sensory decisions by biasing the decision process.
source: This change in probability may affect sensory decisions by directing spatial attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Liston and Stone, 2008) and by biasing the decision process (Hanks et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a study on decision biases.

claim: Changes in probability modify the expected value of choices.
source: It modifies the expected value of the choices, echoing changes in reward probability or size, which affect perceptual choices (e.g. Feng et al., 2009; Whiteley and Sahani, 2008) and drive value-based choices (Corrado et al., 2005; Fan et al., 2018; Herrnstein, 1961; Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on value-based decision-making.

claim: Mice detect the presence of a visual grating to their left or right in the task.
source: In the task, mice detect the presence of a visual grating to their left or right, and report the perceived location with a simple movement: by turning a steering wheel (Burgess et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct description of the task design.

claim: Mice report the perceived location by turning a steering wheel.
source: In the task, mice detect the presence of a visual grating to their left or right, and report the perceived location with a simple movement: by turning a steering wheel (Burgess et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct description of the task design, supported by a citation to the original task.

claim: Task difficulty is controlled by varying the contrast across trials.
source: The task difficulty is controlled by varying the contrast across trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of how task difficulty is manipulated.

claim: The reward for a correct response is a drop of sugar water that is not contingent on licking the spout.
source: The reward for a correct response is a drop of sugar water that is not contingent on licking the spout.
evidence: This is a direct description of the reward structure in the task.

claim: The probability of stimulus appearance at the two locations is asymmetric and changes across blocks of trials.
source: The probability of stimulus appearance at the two locations is asymmetric and changes across blocks of trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of the block structure in the full task.

claim: When the visual stimulus is evident (contrast is high), mice should mostly use vision.
source: When the visual stimulus is evident (contrast is high), they should mostly use vision, and when the visual stimulus is ambiguous (contrast is low or zero), they should consider prior information (Whiteley and Sahani, 2008) and choose the side that has recently been more likely.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected optimal strategy, supported by a citation.

claim: When the visual stimulus is ambiguous (contrast is low or zero), mice should consider prior information and choose the side that has recently been more likely.
source: When the visual stimulus is evident (contrast is high), they should mostly use vision, and when the visual stimulus is ambiguous (contrast is low or zero), they should consider prior information (Whiteley and Sahani, 2008) and choose the side that has recently been more likely.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected optimal strategy, supported by a citation.

claim: In all laboratories, most mice learned the task, although often at a different pace.
source: In all laboratories, most mice learned the task, although often at a different pace.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: After learning, mice performed the task in a comparable manner, with no significant difference across laboratories.
source: After learning they performed the task in a comparable manner, and with no significant difference across laboratories.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses and data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The study established an open-access data architecture pipeline.
source: Following this approach, we established an open-access data architecture pipeline (Bonacchi et al., 2020) and use it to release the >5 million mouse choices at data.internationalbrainlab.org.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data sharing infrastructure, supported by a citation.

claim: The data is released at data.internationalbrainlab.org.
source: Following this approach, we established an open-access data architecture pipeline (Bonacchi et al., 2020) and use it to release the >5 million mouse choices at data.internationalbrainlab.org.
evidence: This is a direct statement about where the data is available.

claim: A complex mouse behavior can be successfully reproduced across laboratories.
source: These results reveal that a complex mouse behavior can be successfully reproduced across laboratories, enabling collaborative studies of brain function in behaving mice.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Four mice were excluded out of 210 due to adverse effects such as developing a cataract during surgery or pain after surgery or substantial weight loss following water control.
source: Throughout these steps, we checked for adverse effects such as developing a cataract during surgery or pain after surgery or substantial weight loss following water control (four mice excluded out of 210) (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about exclusion criteria and numbers, supported by a citation to the water control method.

claim: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task.
source: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task, and 98 in the full task (see Appendix 1—table 1d for training progression and proficiency criteria).
evidence: This is a direct statement about training outcomes.

claim: Out of 206 mice that started training, 98 achieved proficiency in the full task.
source: Out of 206 mice that started training, 140 achieved proficiency in the basic task, and 98 in the full task (see Appendix 1—table 1d for training progression and proficiency criteria).
evidence: This is a direct statement about training outcomes.

claim: The basic task is purely perceptual: the only informative cue is the visual stimulus.
source: The basic task is purely perceptual: the only informative cue is the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct description of the basic task design.

claim: The full task invites integration of perception with recent experience.
source: The full task instead invites integration of perception with recent experience: when stimuli are ambiguous it is best to choose the more likely option.
evidence: This is a direct description of the full task design and optimal strategy.

claim: The study standardized multiple variables including mouse strain and provider, age range, weight range, water access, food protein, and fat.
source: By providing standards and guidelines, we sought to control variables such as mouse strain and provider, age range, weight range, water access, food protein, and fat.
evidence: This is a direct statement about standardization efforts.

claim: The study did not attempt to standardize variables such as light-dark cycle, temperature, humidity, and environmental sound, but documented and measured them regularly.
source: We did not attempt to standardize other variables such as light-dark cycle, temperature, humidity, and environmental sound, but we documented and measured them regularly (Appendix 1—table 1a; Voelkl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement about which variables were not standardized but were monitored.

claim: Data were shared and processed across the collaboration according to a standardized web-based pipeline.
source: Data were shared and processed across the collaboration according to a standardized web-based pipeline (Bonacchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data management, supported by a citation.

claim: The visual stimulus is a grating that appeared at variable contrast on the left or right half of the screen.
source: The visual stimulus, a grating, appeared at variable contrast on the left or right half of the screen.
evidence: This is a direct description of the visual stimulus.

claim: The stimulus position was coupled with movements of the response wheel.
source: The stimulus position was coupled with movements of the response wheel, and mice indicated their choices by turning the wheel left or right to bring the grating to the center of the screen (Burgess et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct description of the task mechanics, supported by a citation.

claim: Trials began after the mouse held the wheel still for 0.4–0.7 s.
source: Trials began after the mouse held the wheel still for 0.4–0.7 s and were announced by an auditory 'go cue'.
evidence: This is a direct description of the trial structure.

claim: Correct decisions were rewarded with sweetened water (10% sucrose solution).
source: Correct decisions were rewarded with sweetened water (10% sucrose solution), whereas incorrect decisions were indicated by a noise burst and were followed by a longer inter-trial interval (2 s) (Guo et al., 2014, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the reward structure, supported by a citation.

claim: Incorrect decisions were indicated by a noise burst and were followed by a longer inter-trial interval (2 s).
source: Correct decisions were rewarded with sweetened water (10% sucrose solution), whereas incorrect decisions were indicated by a noise burst and were followed by a longer inter-trial interval (2 s) (Guo et al., 2014, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the feedback for incorrect responses, supported by a citation and figure reference.

claim: The training proceeded in automated steps, following predefined criteria.
source: The training proceeded in automated steps, following predefined criteria (Figure 1d, IBL Protocol for mice training).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training procedure, supported by a figure and protocol reference.

claim: Initially, mice experienced only easy trials with highly visible stimuli (100% and 50% contrast).
source: Initially, mice experienced only easy trials with highly visible stimuli (100% and 50% contrast).
evidence: This is a direct description of the initial training phase.

claim: As performance improved, the stimulus set progressively grew to include contrasts of 25%, 12%, 6%, and finally 0%.
source: As performance improved, the stimulus set progressively grew to include contrasts of 25%, 12%, 6%, and finally 0% (Figure 1d, Appendix 1—table 1b-c).
evidence: This is a direct description of the training progression, supported by a figure and appendix reference.

claim: Stimuli with contrast >0 could appear on the left or the right and thus appeared twice more often than stimuli with 0% contrast.
source: Stimuli with contrast >0 could appear on the left or the right and thus appeared twice more often than stimuli with 0% contrast.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus presentation probabilities.

claim: For a typical mouse, stimuli with 25% contrast were introduced in training day 10, 12% contrast in Day 12, and the remaining contrasts in Day 13.
source: For a typical mouse (Figure 1d), according to this automated schedule, stimuli with 25% contrast were introduced in training day 10, 12% contrast in Day 12, and the remaining contrasts in Day 13.
evidence: This is a direct description of the training progression for the example mouse, supported by a figure reference.

claim: To reduce response biases, incorrect responses on easy trials (high contrast) were more likely to be followed by a 'repeat trial' with the same stimulus contrast and location.
source: To reduce response biases, incorrect responses on easy trials (high contrast) were more likely to be followed by a 'repeat trial' with the same stimulus contrast and location.
evidence: This is a direct description of the bias correction procedure.

claim: On each training day, mice were typically trained in a single uninterrupted session.
source: On each training day, mice were typically trained in a single uninterrupted session, whose duration depended on performance (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a direct description of the training schedule, supported by a figure reference.

claim: Sessions lasted at most 90 min and ended according to a criterion based on number of trials, total duration, and response times.
source: Sessions lasted at most 90 min and ended according to a criterion based on number of trials, total duration, and response times (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct description of the session ending criteria, supported by a figure reference.

claim: The criterion to end a session was not mandatory: some sessions were ended earlier (5,316/10,903 sessions) and others ended later (5,587/10,903 sessions).
source: The criterion to end a session was not mandatory: some sessions were ended earlier (5,316/10,903 sessions) and others ended later (5,587/10,903 sessions).
evidence: This is a direct statement about session ending practices with specific numbers.

claim: Sessions that continued past the criterion typically continued for an extra 19 ± 16 trials (median ±m.a.d., 5,587 sessions).
source: The latter sessions typically continued for an extra 19 ± 16 trials (median ±m.a.d., 5,587 sessions) longer.
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures.

claim: At the beginning of training, the wheel gain was high (8 deg/mm), making the stimuli highly responsive to small wheel movements.
source: At the beginning of training, the wheel gain was high (8 deg/mm), making the stimuli highly responsive to small wheel movements, and rewards were large (3 μL).
evidence: This is a direct description of the initial training parameters.

claim: At the beginning of training, rewards were large (3 μL).
source: At the beginning of training, the wheel gain was high (8 deg/mm), making the stimuli highly responsive to small wheel movements, and rewards were large (3 μL).
evidence: This is a direct description of the initial reward size.

claim: Once a session had >200 complete trials, the wheel gain was halved to 4 deg/mm and the reward was progressively decreased to 1.5 μL.
source: Once a session had >200 complete trials, the wheel gain was halved to 4 deg/mm and the reward was progressively decreased to 1.5 μL (Appendix 1—table 1b-c).
evidence: This is a direct description of the parameter changes during training, supported by an appendix reference.

claim: Mouse performance gradually improved until it provided high-quality visual psychometric curves.
source: Mouse performance gradually improved until it provided high-quality visual psychometric curves (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a direct statement about training outcomes, supported by a figure reference.

claim: At first, performance hovered around or below 50%.
source: At first, performance hovered around or below 50%.
evidence: This is a direct description of initial performance levels.

claim: Performance could be even below 50% because of no-response trials, systematic response biases, and the bias-correcting procedure that tended to repeat trials following errors on easy trials.
source: It could be even below 50% because of no-response trials (which were labeled as incorrect trials in our analyses), systematic response biases, and the bias-correcting procedure that tended to repeat trials following errors on easy trials (at high contrast).
evidence: This is an explanation for why performance could be below chance, based on the task design.

claim: Performance typically increased over days to weeks until mice made only rare mistakes (lapses) on easy trials.
source: Performance then typically increased over days to weeks until mice made only rare mistakes (lapses) on easy trials (e.g. Figure 1f, Day 14).
evidence: This is a direct description of training progression, supported by a figure reference.

claim: Animals were considered to have reached proficiency in the basic task when they had been introduced to all contrast levels and had met predefined performance criteria.
source: Animals were considered to have reached proficiency in the basic task when they had been introduced to all contrast levels, and had met predefined performance criteria based on the parameters of the psychometric curves fitted to the data (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proficiency criteria.

claim: The proficiency criteria included a maximum absolute value of response bias of <16% contrast.
source: These parameters and the associated criteria were as follows: (1) response bias (estimated from the horizontal position of the psychometric curve): maximum absolute value of <16% contrast; (2) contrast sensitivity (estimated from the slope of the psychometric curve): maximum threshold (1/sensitivity) of 19% contrast; (3) lapse rates (estimated from the asymptotes of the psychometric curve): maximum of 0.2 for their sum.
evidence: This is a direct statement of one of the proficiency criteria.

claim: The proficiency criteria included a maximum contrast threshold of 19%.
source: These parameters and the associated criteria were as follows: (1) response bias (estimated from the horizontal position of the psychometric curve): maximum absolute value of <16% contrast; (2) contrast sensitivity (estimated from the slope of the psychometric curve): maximum threshold (1/sensitivity) of 19% contrast; (3) lapse rates (estimated from the asymptotes of the psychometric curve): maximum of 0.2 for their sum.
evidence: This is a direct statement of one of the proficiency criteria.

claim: The proficiency criteria included a maximum sum of lapse rates of 0.2.
source: These parameters and the associated criteria were as follows: (1) response bias (estimated from the horizontal position of the psychometric curve): maximum absolute value of <16% contrast; (2) contrast sensitivity (estimated from the slope of the psychometric curve): maximum threshold (1/sensitivity) of 19% contrast; (3) lapse rates (estimated from the asymptotes of the psychometric curve): maximum of 0.2 for their sum.
evidence: This is a direct statement of one of the proficiency criteria.

claim: These criteria had to be fulfilled on three consecutive training sessions.
source: These criteria had to be fulfilled on three consecutive training sessions (Figure 1 , Appendix 1—table d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proficiency criteria.

claim: There was substantial variation among mice in learning speed, with the fastest learner achieving basic task proficiency in 3 days, and the slowest after 59 days.
source: There was substantial variation among mice, with the fastest learner achieving basic task proficiency in 3 days, and the slowest after 59 days (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the range of learning speeds, supported by a figure reference.

claim: Estimates of contrast threshold did not vary much during training, with an interquartile range that slightly decreased from 12–29% during the first 10 training days, and 11–23% thereafter.
source: Estimates of contrast threshold did not vary much during training (Figure 2b), with an interquartile range that slightly decreased from 12–29% during the first 10 training days, and 11–23% thereafter.
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures, supported by a figure reference.

claim: Bias did not vary much during training, with an interquartile range of −5.2% to 7.1% during the first 10 days to −5.6% to 6.5% thereafter.
source: Likewise, bias did not vary much, with an interquartile range of −5.2% to 7.1% during the first 10 days to −5.6% to 6.5% thereafter (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures, supported by a figure reference.

claim: The average training took 18.4 ± 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140).
source: The average training took 18.4 ± 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140, Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures, supported by a figure reference.

claim: The number of days needed to achieve basic task proficiency was different across laboratories (p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test followed by a post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
source: The number of days needed to achieve basic task proficiency was different across laboratories (Figure 2g, p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric test followed by a post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical finding, supported by a figure reference and specific statistical test.

claim: Some labs had homogeneous learning rates (e.g. Lab two within-lab interquartile range of 8 days).
source: Some labs had homogeneous learning rates (e.g. Lab two within-lab interquartile range of 8 days), while other labs had larger variability (e.g. Lab six interquartile range of 22 days).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific examples and statistical measures.

claim: Other labs had larger variability in learning rates (e.g. Lab six interquartile range of 22 days).
source: Some labs had homogeneous learning rates (e.g. Lab two within-lab interquartile range of 8 days), while other labs had larger variability (e.g. Lab six interquartile range of 22 days).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific examples and statistical measures.

claim: For mice that learned the task, the average training took 10.8 ± 8.6 thousands of trials (s.d., n = 140).
source: For mice that learned the task, the average training took 10.8 ± 8.6 thousands of trials (s.d., n = 140), similar to the 13 thousand trials of the example mouse from Lab 1 (Figure 2a, black).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures.

claim: The fastest learner met training criteria in one thousand trials, the slowest 43 thousand trials.
source: The fastest learner met training criteria in one thousand trials, the slowest 43 thousand trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the range of learning speeds measured in trials.

claim: To reach 80% on easy trials took on average ~7.4 thousand trials.
source: To reach 80% on easy trials took on average ~7.4 thousand trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement with a specific measure.

claim: Mice across laboratories were not systematically biased towards a particular side and the absolute bias was similar across laboratories (9.8 ± 12.1 [s.d.] on average).
source: Mice across laboratories were not systematically biased towards a particular side and the absolute bias was similar across laboratories (9.8 ± 12.1 [s.d.] on average).
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures.

claim: Measures of contrast threshold stabilized after the first ~10 sessions, which was on average 17.8 ± 11.7% on average across institutions.
source: Likewise, measures of contrast threshold stabilized after the first ~10 sessions, which was on average 17.8 ± 11.7% on average across institutions.
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures.

claim: The variability in performance across mice decreased as training progressed, but it did not disappear.
source: The variability in performance across mice decreased as training progressed, but it did not disappear (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a figure reference.

claim: Between training days 15 and 40, when the average performance on easy trials of the mice increased from 80.7% to 91.1%, the variation across mice (s.d.) of performance on easy trials decreased from 19.1% to 10.1%.
source: For example, between training days 15 and 40, when the average performance on easy trials of the mice increased from 80.7% to 91.1%, the variation across mice (s.d.) of performance on easy trials decreased from 19.1% to 10.1%.
evidence: This is a direct statement with specific statistical measures.

claim: A Random Forests decoder applied to change in performance in the first five sessions was able to predict whether a mouse would end up in the bottom quartile of learning speed with accuracy of 53% (where chance is 25%).
source: A Random Forests decoder applied to change in performance (% correct with easy, high-contrast stimuli) in the first five sessions was able to predict whether a mouse would end up in the bottom quartile of learning speed (the slowest learners) with accuracy of 53% (where chance is 25%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a machine learning analysis result.

claim: The chance of misclassifying a fast-learning, top quartile mouse as a slow-learning, bottom quartile mouse, was only 7%.
source: Conversely, the chance of misclassifying a fast-learning, top quartile mouse as a slow-learning, bottom quartile mouse, was only 7%.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a machine learning analysis result.

claim: There was a 80% probability that mice would learn the task within the 40 days that were usually allotted.
source: Indeed, there was a 80% probability that mice would learn the task within the 40 days that were usually allotted, and when mice were trained for a longer duration, the success rate rose even further (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a figure reference.

claim: When mice were trained for a longer duration than 40 days, the success rate rose even further.
source: Indeed, there was a 80% probability that mice would learn the task within the 40 days that were usually allotted, and when mice were trained for a longer duration, the success rate rose even further (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a figure reference.

claim: Once mice achieved basic task proficiency, multiple measures of performance became indistinguishable across laboratories.
